about.title: About WatchWise
about.description: WatchWise is a free movie and TV discovery guide that combines AI recommendations with trailers, cast and crew, episode ratings, release calendars and where-to-watch information.

sections.heading: Why we built WatchWise
paragraphs: Most evenings, deciding what to watch takes longer than it should. Streaming catalogs are huge, recommendations are tuned to keep you inside one service, and the information you need to decide — who made it, whether the later seasons hold up, whether it is even available where you live — is scattered across many sites.

WatchWise puts that information in one place and adds a recommendation assistant that explains its reasoning. Instead of an endless grid of posters, you can describe the kind of night you are having and get one confident suggestion, together with the reason it fits.

sections.heading: What you can do here
paragraphs: Browse trending, top-rated, upcoming and now-playing titles; filter the catalog by genre, decade, rating, runtime, original language and the streaming services available in your country; read full cast and crew credits and jump to anyone's filmography; watch trailers and featurettes; compare every episode of a series in an episode-ratings heatmap; and follow a weekly release calendar for theaters and TV.

With a free account you can keep a watchlist, mark titles as watched, rate them, pin favorites, follow other viewers, comment on titles and build an AI taste profile that summarizes what you tend to enjoy.

sections.heading: Where our data comes from
paragraphs: Title, people and image data come from The Movie Database (TMDB), a community-built database maintained by film and TV fans around the world. Streaming availability is provided by JustWatch through TMDB. WatchWise uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by TMDB.

Recommendations, taste summaries and editorial guides are written or generated by WatchWise. AI suggestions are a starting point, not a review: we always link to the full title page so you can check the details yourself.

sections.heading: How WatchWise is funded
paragraphs: WatchWise is free to use. To cover hosting and data costs the site may show advertising served by Google AdSense. Ads are clearly separated from recommendations, and advertisers have no influence over which titles we suggest or how they are ranked. You can read how advertising cookies work in our privacy policy.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.description: Answers about WatchWise accounts, AI recommendations, streaming availability, ratings, privacy and advertising.

items.a: Yes. Browsing, searching, trailers, calendars and title pages are free without an account. A free account adds a watchlist, ratings, favorites, following, comments and the AI taste profile.

items.q: Can I watch movies on WatchWise?
items.a: No. WatchWise is a discovery guide, not a streaming service. Each title page shows where the title is available to stream, rent or buy in your country, with a link to the provider.

items.q: How does the AI pick work?
items.a: You describe what you want in plain language. The assistant considers your request together with the genres and titles in your watchlist and favorites, suggests one title, and explains why. The suggestion is then matched to the real TMDB entry so you always land on an accurate title page.

items.q: Why does streaming availability differ from what I see in my app?
items.a: Availability changes often and differs by country. WatchWise shows JustWatch data for the region you choose in the region picker. If something looks out of date, check the provider directly; licensing changes can take a day or two to appear.

The score shown on posters and title pages is the TMDB community average from 0 to 10, with the number of votes next to it where available. Your own 1–5 star ratings are personal and are used to shape your taste profile.

items.q: What is the episode ratings heatmap?
items.a: For TV series, every episode is shown as a coloured square by season, so you can see at a glance whether a show improves, dips or ends strongly. Hover or tap a square to see the episode title and air date.

items.q: How do I change my streaming country?
items.a: Use the globe selector next to “Where to watch” on any title page, on the release calendar, or in the Discover streaming filter. Your choice is remembered on this device.

items.q: Can other people see my watchlist?
items.a: Only if you allow it. Watchlist and activity visibility can be changed in your profile settings at any time.

Advertising helps keep WatchWise free. Ads are served by Google AdSense and never influence recommendations. You can control personalised advertising through Google’s Ad Settings, as described in our privacy policy.

items.q: How do I report a problem or a wrong detail?
items.a: Use the contact page. For incorrect title information you can also edit the entry directly on TMDB, since that is where our catalog data comes from.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.description: How WatchWise collects, uses and protects your information, including cookies and Google AdSense advertising.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: This policy explains what information WatchWise collects when you use the website, how it is used, and the choices you have. By using WatchWise you agree to the practices described here.

sections.heading: Information you provide
paragraphs: When you create an account we store your name, email address, an optional profile photo and an encrypted password. When you use the service we store the titles you add to your watchlist, ratings, favorites, comments, the people you follow and your profile settings. Prompts you send to the AI assistant are processed to generate a recommendation.

sections.heading: Information collected automatically
paragraphs: Like most websites, our servers and service providers receive technical information such as your IP address, browser type, device type, pages visited and the time of each request. We use this to operate the site, keep it secure and understand which features are used.
We store a session cookie to keep you signed in. Your browser’s local storage may also hold convenience settings such as your streaming region and recent searches; these stay on your device.

sections.heading: Advertising and Google AdSense
paragraphs: WatchWise uses Google AdSense to show advertisements. Third-party vendors, including Google, use cookies to serve ads based on your prior visits to this website and other websites.

Google’s use of advertising cookies enables it and its partners to serve ads to you based on your visits to WatchWise and/or other sites on the Internet. You may opt out of personalised advertising by visiting Google Ads Settings (https://adssettings.google.com). You can also opt out of some third-party vendors’ use of cookies for personalised advertising at www.aboutads.info.

For visitors in the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom and Switzerland, ads are shown in line with Google’s EU user consent policy, and you may be asked to choose your consent preferences. More information on how Google uses data is available at https://policies.google.com/technologies/partner-sites.

sections.heading: How we use information
paragraphs: We use information to provide and improve WatchWise, personalise recommendations and your taste profile, show your activity to people you allow, prevent abuse, and respond to messages. We do not sell your personal information.

sections.heading: Service providers
paragraphs: We rely on trusted providers to run WatchWise: hosting and database providers, an AI provider that processes recommendation prompts, an image host for profile photos, The Movie Database (TMDB) for catalog data, and Google AdSense for advertising. They process data only as needed to provide their services.

sections.heading: Data retention and your choices
paragraphs: We keep account data for as long as your account is active. You can edit your profile, change visibility settings, remove watchlist items and comments, or ask us to delete your account at any time through the contact page. You can block or delete cookies in your browser settings; some features, such as staying signed in, need cookies to work.

sections.heading: Children
paragraphs: WatchWise is not directed to children under 13, and we do not knowingly collect personal information from them. If you believe a child has created an account, please contact us and we will remove it.

sections.heading: Changes and contact
paragraphs: We may update this policy as the service changes; the date at the top shows the latest revision. Questions about privacy can be sent through the contact page.

guides.title: How to pick a movie for your mood in five minutes
guides.description: A practical method for choosing something to watch tonight without scrolling for an hour: name the mood, set two limits, and shortlist three.

sections.heading: Start with the feeling, not the genre
paragraphs: Genres describe what a film is about; moods describe what it does to you. A thriller can be a comfort watch if you have seen it five times, and a comedy can be exhausting at the end of a long week. Before opening any app, finish the sentence “Tonight I want to feel…” — calm, thrilled, moved, curious, scared, or simply entertained without thinking.

That one word removes most of the catalog. It also gives a recommendation assistant something far more useful than “a good movie”. On WatchWise you can type the sentence exactly as you said it, for example “something warm and funny that I can half-watch while cooking”.

sections.heading: Set two practical limits
paragraphs: The first limit is time. A 95-minute film and a 160-minute epic are different commitments; decide which one you have energy for. The second limit is access: only consider titles on services you already pay for, or that you are happy to rent. In Discover, the runtime chips and the streaming filter handle both in two clicks.

Limits feel restrictive but they are what make decisions fast. Research on choice overload consistently finds that people are more satisfied when they choose from a short list than from an enormous one.

sections.heading: Shortlist three, then decide with the trailer
paragraphs: Add three candidates to your watchlist instead of opening each one. Then compare them side by side: the synopsis, the score and number of votes, and the first thirty seconds of each trailer. Trailers are designed to sell, but tone is hard to fake — if the music and pacing do not match your mood, move on.
If two options are still tied, pick the one you would be more annoyed to have missed. Save the other for next time; that is what the watchlist is for.

sections.heading: Make the next decision easier
paragraphs: After watching, take five seconds to rate the title. Ratings feed your taste profile, so the next suggestion starts from what you actually enjoyed rather than what is popular this week. Over a few weeks you will notice the shortlist step getting shorter.

guides.title: Film and TV genres explained: what each one promises
guides.description: A plain-language guide to the major genres and subgenres, what experience each one promises, and how to use them to find titles you will enjoy.

sections.heading: A genre is a promise
paragraphs: Every genre makes an implicit promise to the audience. A mystery promises a puzzle that will be solved; a romance promises that the relationship is the point; a horror film promises tension and release. Knowing the promise helps you predict whether a title will satisfy you, even when you have never heard of it.

sections.heading: Drama, comedy and their many mixes
paragraphs: Drama focuses on characters facing serious, believable problems, and its reward is emotional truth. Comedy promises laughter but also lightness: stakes may be real, but the tone reassures you things will be fine. Many of the most loved titles live in between — the “dramedy” — where humour makes painful material easier to watch.
When filtering, combining genres narrows results in useful ways. Drama plus Crime tends to produce character-driven detective stories; Comedy plus Animation skews toward family viewing.

sections.heading: Thriller, mystery and crime
paragraphs: These three overlap but differ in focus. A mystery asks “who did it?” and plays fair with clues. A thriller asks “will they survive?” and is built on suspense and momentum. Crime stories ask “how and why?” and often follow the people committing the crime rather than those solving it. If you enjoy working things out, lean toward mystery; if you want your pulse raised, choose thriller.

sections.heading: Science fiction and fantasy
paragraphs: Science fiction explores a “what if” rooted in technology or science — artificial intelligence, space travel, time loops — and the best examples use the idea to say something about people today. Fantasy builds worlds with their own rules, often drawing on myth. Both genres reward patience: the first episode or act usually spends time explaining the world, so judge a series after two or three episodes rather than one.

sections.heading: Horror and its quieter cousins
paragraphs: Horror ranges from jump scares to slow, atmospheric dread. Subgenres matter a lot here: supernatural horror, slashers, psychological horror and folk horror deliver very different experiences. If you dislike gore but enjoy unease, try psychological horror or a “slow-burn” mystery with dark themes.
Use the keyword links on each title page to find more titles with the same specific ingredients — a haunted house, a time loop, a heist — rather than relying on the broad genre alone.

sections.heading: Documentary and animation are formats, not moods
paragraphs: Documentaries can be thrillers, comedies or tragedies; animation can be for toddlers or adults only. Treat them as formats and combine them with a mood or genre filter to get closer to what you want.

guides.title: Finding hidden gems: well-loved titles most people missed
guides.description: How to discover excellent movies and series that never trended, using ratings, vote counts, languages and decades instead of popularity.

sections.heading: Why great titles get buried
paragraphs: Popularity lists reward marketing budgets and recency. A small film released in a crowded week, a series from a country you rarely browse, or a classic that predates streaming can all be excellent and still never appear on a trending row. Finding them means changing what you sort by.

sections.heading: Read the score together with the vote count
paragraphs: A 9.2 from twelve votes says very little; a 7.8 from three thousand votes is a strong signal. When you browse by rating, set a minimum number of votes so a handful of enthusiastic fans cannot push an obscure title to the top. WatchWise’s Hidden gems switch does this for you: it sorts by rating while requiring a meaningful number of votes.

sections.heading: Change one dimension at a time
paragraphs: Try the same genre in a different decade, or the same mood in a different original language. Korean thrillers, Spanish-language mysteries, French dramas and Japanese animation each have deep catalogs that rarely surface in English-language trending lists. In Discover, pick one genre, then switch the language or decade chips and compare the results.
Another reliable route is people. When you love a film, open the director’s or writer’s page and look at their earlier work; first features are often smaller, stranger and less seen.

sections.heading: Follow keywords, studios and networks
paragraphs: Every title page lists keywords and the studios or networks behind it, and each one is clickable. Small production companies often have a recognisable style, so if one surprising film came from a particular studio, its catalog is a good place to look for the next.

guides.title: Only see what you can actually watch: using streaming filters
guides.description: How streaming availability works by country, how to filter by the services you pay for, and why availability changes.

sections.heading: Availability depends on where you are
paragraphs: Streaming rights are sold country by country, so the same service can carry very different catalogs in Egypt, the United Kingdom and the United States. That is why WatchWise asks for your region. Choose it once with the globe selector and every title page, the Discover streaming filter and the release calendar will use it.

sections.heading: Stream, free, rent or buy
paragraphs: On each title page, offers are grouped by type. “Stream” means included in a subscription. “Free” covers services that are free with ads. “Rent” and “Buy” are one-off purchases. If a title only appears under rent or buy, it may arrive on a subscription service later — add it to your watchlist and check back.

sections.heading: Filter by the services you pay for
paragraphs: In Discover, open Filters and select the logos of your services. Results are then limited to titles available on any of them in your region, and you can still combine the filter with genres, decades, rating and runtime. It is the quickest way to turn a long list into a list you can press play on.

sections.heading: Why the information can lag
paragraphs: Catalogs change every day, especially at the start of each month. Availability data is provided by JustWatch and usually updates within a day, but always confirm in the provider’s app before planning a movie night around a specific title.

guides.title: How to build a watchlist you will actually finish
guides.description: Simple habits for keeping a watchlist short, varied and useful, so it helps you decide instead of becoming another endless list.

sections.heading: A watchlist is a menu, not a museum
paragraphs: Most watchlists grow forever because adding is easy and removing feels like losing something. A useful list is short enough to scan in one glance — roughly twenty to forty titles. Anything beyond that is a backlog, and backlogs make choosing harder, not easier.

sections.heading: Keep a mix of commitments
paragraphs: Balance the list across effort levels: a few short comfort watches, a few demanding films for when you have energy, and one or two series you are actively following. When you open the list on a tired Tuesday, there should be an obvious easy option.

sections.heading: Review it once a month
paragraphs: Once a month, remove anything you no longer feel excited about. If you hesitate, ask whether you would add it today; if not, let it go. Mark finished titles as watched and rate them — the rating is quick, and it improves future recommendations far more than adding new titles does.

sections.heading: Use favorites for the titles that define your taste
paragraphs: Favorites are different from the watchlist: they are the handful of titles you would recommend to anyone. Pinning them on your profile helps friends understand your taste and gives the AI a strong signal about what you value in a story.
